package_info.package_versions: unknown (all distributed versions as of June 2020)
package_info.why_malicious: GoldenSpy is malicious because it installs a covert backdoor component alongside legitimate tax software, enabling remote attackers to execute arbitrary code, maintain persistent unauthorized access, and evade removal by surviving uninstallation of the main application. This represents a severe supply-chain compromise with high risk of data exfiltration and system control.

execution_context.trigger: post-installation runtime (background process launched after tax software installation)
execution_context.file_location: GoldenSpy installation directory (e.g., %ProgramFiles%\GoldenSpy\ or similar, as a separate executable or DLL)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The backdoor component is installed as a separate executable or DLL in the tax software's directory. Upon installation, it launches as a background process, establishes a persistent outbound connection to a hardcoded remote command-and-control (C2) server, and enters a loop where it receives and executes arbitrary commands from the attacker, returning results over the network.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ or C# (Windows executable or DLL, as identified in forensic analysis)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At post-installation runtime, the code launches as a hidden background process, establishes a persistent TCP connection to a hardcoded C2 server, receives attacker-supplied commands, executes them locally (including process creation and file operations), and transmits execution results back to the C2 server, enabling full remote control.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code creates a covert, unauthorized remote access channel that operates independently of the main application, allowing attackers to execute arbitrary code and control the system without user knowledge or consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate tax software should not install hidden background processes that communicate with external servers or execute remote commands. All network activity and process creation should be transparent and limited to documented, user-initiated functions.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Remote administration tools in enterprise environments, but only when explicitly installed, documented, and consented to by the user or IT staff.
key_indicators: Hidden persistent process (e.g., 'svprc.exe') running from the tax software directory
Outbound network connections to hardcoded or unlisted C2 domains/IPs
Ability to receive and execute arbitrary code or shell commands from the network
Process auto-start via registry or scheduled task entries

execution_context.trigger: post-uninstallation (after user removes main tax software)
execution_context.file_location: GoldenSpy installation directory (malicious executable or DLL remains after main app uninstall, e.g., %ProgramFiles%\GoldenSpy\)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: After the main tax software is uninstalled, the backdoor executable or DLL remains in the installation directory and continues to run as a background process, maintaining its persistence mechanisms (such as registry run keys or scheduled tasks) to ensure it is automatically launched on system startup.
malicious_snippets.code_language: C++ or C# (Windows executable or DLL)
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At post-uninstallation, the code persists as a hidden background process by maintaining registry run keys or scheduled tasks, continues to run from the original installation directory, and retains remote access capabilities for the attacker, enabling ongoing unauthorized control and potential data exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Persistence after uninstallation is a hallmark of malware, as it ensures continued unauthorized access even after the user believes the software has been removed. The lack of user notification and deliberate evasion of removal mechanisms are clear indicators of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal software should remove all components and persistence mechanisms upon uninstallation, leaving no residual executables or background processes.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System management agents may persist after application removal, but only with explicit user awareness, documentation, and consent.
key_indicators: Malicious executable or DLL remains in installation directory after main app uninstall
Persistence mechanisms (e.g., registry run keys, scheduled tasks) remain active post-uninstall
No user notification or visible indication of remaining components
Background process continues to run and communicate externally after uninstall

attack_chain.action: User installs the official tax software, which silently deploys the GoldenSpy backdoor component as a separate executable or DLL in the installation directory.
attack_chain.leads_to: Backdoor process is established and begins persistent communication with the remote C2 server.

attack_chain.action: The backdoor process launches as a hidden background service, connects to the hardcoded C2 server, and awaits attacker commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker can remotely execute arbitrary code, perform file operations, and control the system.

attack_chain.action: User uninstalls the main tax software, but the backdoor component remains installed and active, maintaining persistence via registry or scheduled tasks.
attack_chain.leads_to: Continued unauthorized remote access, potential data exfiltration, and further compromise even after software removal.

behavioral_signatures: Hidden background process (e.g., 'svprc.exe') running from the tax software installation directory
Outbound TCP connections to hardcoded or suspicious C2 domains/IPs from unknown executables
Persistence mechanisms (registry run keys, scheduled tasks) referencing executables in the tax software directory
Execution of arbitrary code or shell commands received from the network
file_indicators: Unknown executables or DLLs (e.g., 'svprc.exe', 'svprc.dll') present in the tax software installation directory
Files remaining in %ProgramFiles%\GoldenSpy\ or similar directory after tax software uninstall
Registry run keys or scheduled tasks referencing GoldenSpy-related executables
network_indicators: Outbound connections to hardcoded C2 domains/IPs as listed in the report (e.g., 'update.svprc.com', specific IP addresses)
Unusual network traffic from processes not documented as part of the legitimate tax software
Persistent connections to external servers initiated by unknown executables
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for unknown or suspicious processes running from the tax software installation directory, especially those that persist after uninstallation. Inspect for executables or DLLs (e.g., 'svprc.exe') that remain after the main application is removed. Audit registry run keys and scheduled tasks for references to GoldenSpy-related files. Analyze network traffic for outbound connections to hardcoded or suspicious C2 domains/IPs. Use endpoint detection tools to flag processes that execute commands received from the network or maintain persistence after uninstall.
